pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–7 — describe a simple ocean food chain: tiny plants (phytoplankton) → small animals → bigger fish → top predators like sharks, showing all ocean life depends on others for food.
• Standards — UK (DfE KS1): Y2 'describe how animals obtain their food from plants and other animals, using the idea of a simple food chain, and identify and name different sources of food' — this is the ocean instance of the KS1 food-chain objective.
• Standards — US (NGSS): builds toward 5-PS3-1 / 5-LS2-1 (matter and energy movement) but at K–2 the accessible anchor is 'animals get food from plants and other animals' — who-eats-whom sequencing.
• Operational details: teach the ARROW as 'is eaten by' (energy/food flows in the arrow's direction) — the single most important convention and the classic error source. Start the chain with tiny plants (phytoplankton) so children grasp that the ocean, like land, is powered by plants they can barely see. Keep to a clear 3–4 link chain (phytoplankton → small fish/krill → big fish → shark).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete, ~5–6): orders pictures big-eats-small and says 'the shark eats the fish'; Tier B (~6–7): builds a ≥3-link chain and states it starts with tiny plants; Tier C (~7): reads the arrow correctly as 'is eaten by' and explains each animal depends on the one before it.
bestPractices: Define the arrow explicitly as 'is eaten by' and rehearse reading chains aloud in the arrow direction — pre-empt the near-universal 'arrow points to who eats' reversal.
Always begin the chain with a producer (phytoplankton/algae): make visible that even the ocean's food starts with tiny plants using sunlight.
Use physical/manipulable cards the child arranges into order, then link with arrows — building beats being shown a finished chain.
Probe dependence with 'what if?' removal ('if the tiny plants vanished, what happens to the small fish? the shark?') to establish the chain-of-dependence idea (seeds later food-web work).
Use real, recognisable ocean species (phytoplankton, krill/small fish, mackerel, shark) rather than abstract 'small/medium/big'.
keyRepresentations: A left-to-right ocean food chain with clearly labelled 'is eaten by' arrows
Drag-and-arrange picture cards (phytoplankton, small fish, big fish, shark) that snap into a chain
A nested 'who's inside who' cutaway showing energy passing up the chain
A sun → phytoplankton starter icon making the energy source explicit
commonMisconceptions: Arrow reversal: reading the arrow as 'eats' rather than 'is eaten by' — the dominant error in food-chain teaching.
'Ocean food chains start with a big animal' — missing that they start with tiny plants/plankton because those aren't obvious.
'Big/scary animals are the most important' — not seeing that predators depend on everything below them.
Believing the sea has no plants ('there's nothing green down there') so children can't locate the producer.
Thinking each animal eats only one thing / the chain is the whole story (the web extension corrects this later).

learn.summary: Help children aged 5–7 describe a simple ocean food chain: tiny plants (phytoplankton) → small animals (krill/small fish) → bigger fish → top predator (shark). The two core goals are (1) understanding that this ocean food chain STARTS with tiny plants that make their own food from sunlight, and (2) reading the arrow correctly as 'is eaten by' so food/energy flows up the chain toward the eater. A central proposed activity is to have children build a chain from cards, then remove a link to notice that every animal depends on the one below it.

activities.title: Build-and-break the ocean food chain
feedback: If a child puts the shark first because it is biggest/strongest, ask 'what does the shark's dinner eat, and what does THAT eat?' — keep going down until you reach the tiny plant that makes its own food. That base is where the chain starts.

If a child reads or draws the arrow as 'eats' (pointing from predator to prey), re-state the arrow as 'is eaten by' / 'gives its energy to': it points TOWARD the eater. Trace energy flowing UP the chain, not the mouth pointing down.

If a child asks what feeds the phytoplankton, explain that phytoplankton make their own food using sunlight (like plants on land), so they do not need to eat any other living thing — they are the true start of the chain.
When a link is removed and the child notices the animals above lose their food, name it: 'every animal depends on the one below it.'
activities.rationale: This activity instantiates the KS1 objective of describing a simple food chain and centres the phytoplankton producer base that everything else depends on. Constructing and then disrupting the chain lets children build the sequence themselves and reason about dependence, rather than being shown a finished chain, and it rehearses the two common error sources (start-point and arrow direction). Using real, recognisable species keeps it concrete for this age. Efficacy of this specific task is proposed, not empirically validated.
sourceClaims: UK KS1 Y2 science requires pupils to describe how animals obtain food from plants and other animals using the idea of a simple food chain, and to identify and name different sources of food.
Phytoplankton are microscopic marine algae that form the base of the ocean food web, using sunlight to produce food (photosynthesis) — nearly all ocean life ultimately depends on them.
learnerActions: Take a set of picture cards — phytoplankton (tiny sea plants), krill or small fish, a bigger fish (e.g. mackerel), and a shark — and arrange them into who-eats-whom order along a lane.
Place the tiny plants first and say aloud why the chain starts there ('the plants make their own food from sunlight').

Draw or place an arrow between each pair and read the chain aloud in the arrow direction, saying 'is eaten by' at each arrow (phytoplankton is eaten by the small fish, which is eaten by the big fish, which is eaten by the shark).
Remove one card (for example the small fish) and talk through what happens to the animals that depended on it — which ones no longer have food?
activities.intendedInsight: This ocean food chain begins with tiny plants that make their own food from sunlight, and each animal depends on the one before it; the arrow means 'is eaten by' and shows food/energy travelling up toward the eater.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal predator and prey
feedback: If a child names only what an animal eats, prompt 'and what eats IT?' to surface its two-way position in the chain (except the shark, which nothing in this chain eats; and the phytoplankton, which makes its own food and eats nothing).
Reinforce that the arrow reads 'is eaten by' every time, in the same direction.
activities.rationale: A labelled reveal clearly presents the sequence and arrow meaning and is a lower-effort companion to construction. It shows the chain rather than letting the child build it or experience a link being removed, so it works best alongside the build activity. It does not by itself elicit the dependence reasoning.
learnerActions: Look at a pre-drawn ocean food chain with labelled 'is eaten by' arrows.
Tap each animal to reveal what it eats and what eats it, then say the relationship aloud ('the mackerel eats the small fish and is eaten by the shark').
Point along the chain and say which way the food/energy travels.
activities.intendedInsight: The producer (phytoplankton) makes its own food and has nothing below it; each animal above the base has prey below it, and every animal except the top predator also has a predator above it. The arrow consistently points to the eater.

activities.title: Order the chain and explain the arrow
feedback: If the order is wrong, return to building a chain from cards and tracing down to the plant base.
If the arrow is read as 'eats', re-rehearse 'is eaten by' pointing toward the eater.
activities.rationale: A sequencing task plus a direct question on arrow meaning is a tight check of the two core evidence goals. This format confirms the ordered answer and the stated meaning but does not by itself elicit the dependence reasoning that removing a link produces.
learnerActions: Put the pictures in order: phytoplankton → small fish → big fish → shark.
Answer: what does this ocean food chain start with?
Answer: what does the arrow between two animals mean, and which way does it point?
activities.intendedInsight: Confirms the child can both sequence the chain producer-first and state that the arrow means 'is eaten by', pointing to the eater.

activities.title: What-if dependence talk (optional companion)
feedback: If a child says the shark is most important because it is biggest, trace the dependence downward until the plant base is reached.
Keep the conversation anchored to the child's own built or drawn chain so the reasoning stays concrete.
activities.rationale: Removal 'what-if?' questions can establish the chain-of-dependence idea and pre-empt the 'big/scary = most important' misconception. Dialogue is a useful curiosity and reasoning supplement; it supports but does not replace having the child construct the ordered chain.
learnerActions: With a built chain in front of them, discuss: 'If there were no phytoplankton at all, what would happen to the little animals, then the fish, then the shark?'
Discuss 'Which is more important to the whole chain — the shark or the tiny plants? Why?'

If a marine expert or knowledgeable adult is available, ask curiosity questions like 'what does a shark eat, and what does that eat?' and be nudged to keep tracing down until they name the plant at the bottom.
activities.intendedInsight: Removing the producer collapses everything above it, so the tiny plants — not the biggest animal — underpin the whole chain; this seeds later food-web work.

constraints: Keep to a clear 3–4 link chain (phytoplankton → small fish/krill → big fish → shark); avoid longer chains at this age.

Always begin the chain with a producer (phytoplankton/algae) and make the sunlight→plant energy source explicit, so children can locate the producer despite there being 'nothing obviously green' in the sea.
Define the arrow explicitly as 'is eaten by' and rehearse reading chains aloud in the arrow direction to pre-empt the common 'arrow points to who eats' reversal.
Use real, recognisable ocean species rather than abstract 'small/medium/big'.

Recognition/ordering and tap-to-reveal formats confirm the sequence and stated arrow meaning but do not on their own elicit the dependence reasoning; pair them with construction and removal to meet that goal.
The chain simplifies reality (each animal shown eating only one thing); flag that real feeding relationships form a web, to be developed later.
Card or screen pieces are concrete stand-ins for living organisms; the represented organisms, not the pieces, are what depend on each other.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two cited sources were not re-fetched, and both carry verified:false in the source row.
All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions; no empirical efficacy for these specific tasks is claimed.

The original source asserted fixed comparative value for live build/break ('that live recompute is precisely what makes dependence FELT') and that '3D adds nothing'. These format-superiority claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits; the underlying observation that a food chain is a relational rather than spatial structure is retained.

The non-preferred conversation and ordering/check approaches were retained as distinct activities because they serve different purposes (curiosity/reasoning and confirmation) rather than being dropped.

The original diagnostic prompt presents a deliberately wrong chain (shark first, plants last) for the child to critique; this is an assessment design detail, preserved as such and never turned into a learner-facing model of a correct chain.
One source-row reteach prerequisite id is internal routing metadata and was not carried into learner-facing guidance.

Both retained sourceClaims support activity[0] because that activity directly instantiates the describe-a-food-chain objective and teaches the phytoplankton producer base; neither source attests to the efficacy of the build-and-break method itself.

probeDeeper: 'You put the tiny plants first. Where do THEY get their food from — does something feed them?'
'Point along your chain — which way does the food/energy travel, up to the shark or down to the plant?'
'If there were no phytoplankton at all, what would happen to the little animals, and then the fish, and then the shark?' (dependence counterexample)
'Which is more important to the whole chain — the shark or the tiny plants? Why?'
assess.correctAnswer: It's the wrong way round. The chain should START with the tiny sea plants (phytoplankton), because they make their own food from sunlight and everything else depends on them. Then small animals eat the phytoplankton, bigger fish eat the small animals, and the shark (a top predator) comes LAST. The arrows point from the food to the eater (phytoplankton → small animal → fish → shark) and mean 'is eaten by' — they show which way the food/energy goes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Starts the chain with the biggest/strongest animal because it seems most important ('the shark is the boss, so it goes first')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what does the shark's dinner eat, and what does THAT eat?' — keep going down until you reach the tiny plant that makes its own food. That base is where the chain starts.
errorPatterns.distractor: The shark comes first because it's the biggest and strongest
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts the top predator first; treats the plant as least important / last

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the arrows — draws them from the eater to its food ('shark → fish' meaning shark eats fish)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-define the arrow as 'is eaten by' / 'gives its energy to' — it points TOWARD the eater. Trace energy flowing UP the chain, not the mouth pointing down.
errorPatterns.distractor: The arrows point from each animal to the food it eats
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: says the arrow means 'eats', pointing from predator to prey

errorPatterns.pattern: Puts a tiny plant first but thinks something must feed it too — doesn't grasp that plants make their own food
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain phytoplankton make their own food from sunlight (like plants on land) — nothing has to feed them, so they are the true start of the chain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asks what feeds the phytoplankton; looks for an earlier animal before it

responseLevels.gap: Starts with the biggest predator and/or reverses the arrows; sees the plant as unimportant.
responseLevels.full: Starts the chain with phytoplankton (which make their own food), orders small→big to the top predator, states the arrow means 'is eaten by' pointing to the eater, AND reasons about dependence (removing the base collapses the chain) — not a memorised order.
responseLevels.partial: Gets the order roughly right (plants first) OR the arrow meaning, but not both — e.g. starts with phytoplankton yet still points arrows the wrong way, or can't say plants make their own food.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is an ocean food chain someone made: they put the SHARK first because it's the biggest and strongest, then a fish, then tiny sea plants (phytoplankton) last. Is that the right way round? Tell me what should come FIRST in the chain and why, and what the arrows between them mean.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands food chains starts with the producer (tiny plants) and can say the arrow points to the eater. A child who thinks 'most important = first' starts with the biggest/strongest predator, and often reverses the arrows (predator eats prey, so points at prey). The two tiers catch both the start-point error and the arrow-direction error — each a documented, distinct mistake.
